author: jackclarkSF
text: I have an occasional (thankfully) physical ailment which brings all of this into focus: your money, titles, and audience aren't very useful if your body doesn't work. They can't help you. But the stuff in your own head can, and it's all you've actually got when the stakes rise.

author: jackclarkSF
text: The bigger part of this is that: no one can take this stuff away from you. You can lose titles and money and your audience(s). But it's very hard to lose a palace of ideas you've been building in your own brain for decades. These things are what strength derives from.

author: jackclarkSF
text: Of course it'd be nice to be rich, or a famous artist, or have some big title. But I like walking through the streets with a cane, body half-broken, thinking about stories about alien technology inspired by knots I see in trees, or weeds rising up through pavement cracks.

author: jackclarkSF
text: Contemporary society wants you to optimize for a certain kind of tangible success, like money or significant viewership/readership or having certain fancy titles. Personally, I'm more interested in intangible success - stuff where you can lose everything and it's in your head.

author: jackclarkSF
text: @dschatsky I think mental illness is frequently a consequence of an environment in which you're given no chances to 'get out'. Lots of mental illness comes from being stressed and poor and taking the only easy escape options you're given (drugs, etc). I'm not sure much is intrinsic.

author: jackclarkSF
text: The most opinionated way I can put this: Poor people have probably been unlucky through circumstance or through a couple of unwise choices which compounded. Just because someone is on the street, doesn't mean they can't be a genius.

author: jackclarkSF
text: Another way to put this: The reason why homeless people have a hard time lifting themselves out of poverty is that the fact they're homeless deprives them of many of the chances you need to be able to be resourceful. You can't be resourceful if you've given zero opportunities.

author: jackclarkSF
text: People are equally resourceful, if they're given equal chances. Many of the most accomplished people have had a lot of chances to do stuff. Many of the least accomplished have had fewer chances.

author: jackclarkSF
text: If you want to make a real difference in the world, I I think you need to be idiosyncratic about what you do, which means you need to be willing to be weird yourself. Meaningful success mostly correlates to people who show up, day after day, doing something very weird.

author: jackclarkSF
text: So I think it's a good trade - you're going to lose out on some of the success tchotchkes of contemporary life, but you're going to gain in your own idiosyncratic approach to things.

author: jackclarkSF
text: This approach has drawbacks - it doesn't optimize for typical success, or developing fungible skills. But it does create purpose - if you work on stuff for yourself, you're putting yourself on the line, and not an imagery archetype of a successful person. Real stakes.

author: jackclarkSF
text: The personal challenges of my life have been about trying to spend more time doing the things that feel true to me, and less time doing things that I don't believe in. This has also generally correlated to my happiness and the vibrancy of my inner mental world.

author: jackclarkSF
text: You can convince yourself to do things that the world wants you to do rather than what you want to do, but at some point you'll break mental composure and you'll see the joke, which will diminish the quality of your work. You'll also be unhappy.

author: jackclarkSF
text: If you do things for yourself, then you'll keep doing them forever. If you do things because the world says they're what success comes from, then you'll continually assess your skill at them against some goal&benchmark you don't believe in.

author: jackclarkSF
text: Here's a thread about doing things for yourself vs doing things the world thinks you should do. As I've got older, I've noticed that the more time I spend on the things that make sense to me, the more stable and fulfilled I am.

text: But the sad fact is COVID has shown that a lot of older, Western governments have lost their ability to take coordinated, thoughtful actions, both at an administrative level and a technical level. It should trouble us more advanced responses are being fielded elsewhere.

author: jackclarkSF
text: This thread brought to you by a conversation with a family member who explained to me that governments are developing AI technology to embed onto tiny chips that will get injected into us as part of COVID vaccine response. Honestly, I'd almost rather this was true!

author: jackclarkSF
text: I think the 1997 film 'Armageddon' was probably the last time it was feasible to do a mass culture movie where you hint that NASA has secret ultra-advanced spaceships - and the moviegoers believe it! People wouldn't believe it, these days.

author: jackclarkSF
text: This is especially dissonant to me, as I get to work at the border of advanced technology (e.g, @OpenAI ) and government(s). Across the West, most governments have been on a multi-decade outsourcing binge that has reduced their ability to execute in most facets of life.

author: jackclarkSF
text: The most depressing things about conspiracy theories is they tend to rely on governments being incredibly competent, technically advanced, and astonishingly well run. This is rarely the case.

author: jackclarkSF
text: Initiatives like the AI Index give us a chance to prototype aspects of AI measurement and analysis in public, with input from tons of different people. They're also a way to try and take a step back and think more holistically in the field. Please, help us iterate further!

author: jackclarkSF
text: There's also a policy element to this - over time, governments tend to analyze and measure things that influence society (weather, security, energy prices, CCTV cameras, etc). I think measuring AI is hard and there aren't too many obvious best practices.

author: jackclarkSF
text: Why do I think the AI Index is useful? I think it's generally useful to try and measure and analyze aspects of any given technology, and AI is such a rapidly developing field it feels helpful to have a few different initiatives try and measure this stuff.

author: jackclarkSF
text: What kinds of choices do we have about how this unfolds? How can we better guide different states to different outcomes? And how will evolution of technologies that support faster OODA loops, like AI, influence geopolitics here? Trying to do some thinking around this!

author: jackclarkSF
text: I think the long-term implications of this stuff are pretty difficult for people that like democracies, individual sovereignty, and general notions of freedom. There's going to be a significant economic and security-led pressure for states to digitize&analyze everything.

author: jackclarkSF
text: We'll also find some states will adopt surveillance technologies to massively increase the speed of their OODA loops. China does this a ton already with civil-military integration of surveillance tech. But other states are exploring this stuff as well - UK, Taiwan, Singapore, etc

author: jackclarkSF
text: What does this mean? We'll start to look at states in terms of ability to rapidly understand stuff happening around them, analyze that information, and make policy in response (see: various different responses to COVID usually being function of testing/measurement).

author: jackclarkSF
text: Playing around with notion that we'll evaluate 21st century geopolitics through lens of 'information empires'. It's going to be increasingly apparent that AI-driven OODA loops (https://t.co/AQI9TJ00pk) are going to define competitive dynamics in many areas of life.

author: jackclarkSF
text: These 'information architectures' are important because they have significant economic impacts. They're analogous to the brain-nerve relay systems in our bodies that set a ceiling on how fast we can observe and respond to things. And they're constantly changing!

author: jackclarkSF
text: It's not superficially obvious, but all around us companies like @stripe @Google @amazon @Facebook @AlibabaB2B @TencentGlobal @Microsoft etc are building the tools to let them operate at fundamentally different speeds relative to the rest of the world.

text: @cwarzel At @OpenAI we have a pretty decent norm of "no meeting days" across company on Weds/Thurs, and on Policy team (which I lead) we try and chunk our meetings onto one or at most two days a week, which has been helpful for letting people have time for deep/focused work

text: @pcihon @OECD @mmitchell_ai I think certification is ultimately going to arise from a ton of information about how models get used and where they make positive/negative differences , and I think it's super important to encourage more people to try and 'self-certify' stuff.

author: jackclarkSF
text: @pcihon @OECD Regarding certification, I'm mostly going to talk about things like Model Cards (cc @mmitchell_ai ) and other labeling schemes. I think there's huge value in a bottom-up creation of metadata about deployed models, and I'm excited by things like this because is tractable now

author: jackclarkSF
text: @OECD I have a (strangely optimistic) belief that dealing with challenges of tech disruption is surprisingly tractable. What we need is additional government investment, attention & capacity building (think of this as growing a government information 'immune system').
